title: From Atomisation to HTML: My Honest Journey Using AI to Plan Lessons
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele frames AI-assisted lesson planning as a teacher-retention issue, arguing that the burden of resource creation drives trainees and experienced teachers out of the profession. He recounts a hybrid workflow built on Kris Boulton's concept of atomisation, breaking objectives into their smallest chainable atoms, which he encoded into a custom Gemini Gem so the AI does the structural heavy lifting of atomising a topic and drafting full lesson architecture. His honest verdict is mixed: automating slide-deck creation was not worth the effort, so he reverted to making slides by hand, but generating independent-practice resources was a breakthrough, first via LaTeX worksheets and then via clickable HTML worksheets inspired by another Substack writer. The result is a division of labour where AI handles atomisation and planning, the teacher handles visual storytelling, and AI plus code handle worksheet generation.
points: Emanuele treats the resource-creation burden as a retention crisis, arguing schools should provide high-quality pre-planned resources so teachers can focus on delivery and relationships.
He built a custom Gemini Gem trained on Boulton's atomisation principles so AI does the cognitively demanding work of breaking a topic into chainable atoms.
The Gem was upgraded to generate full lesson architecture, teacher scripts, activities, and plenaries, removing blank-page syndrome.
Automating Google Slides from templates proved not worth it, debugging took as long as manual work, so he paused slide automation and kept building slides by hand.
The biggest win was independent-practice resources, via LaTeX PDFs and then clickable HTML worksheets that reveal answers on click.
quotes: The burden of resource creation is driving trainee teachers to quit before they start being teachers and pushing experienced educators out of the profession.
I realised that while AI struggles with “creativity,” it excels at “structure.
It removes the “blank page syndrome” and provides a rigorous pedagogical skeleton for the lesson in seconds.
My honest verdict? Right now, for me, the juice isn’t worth the squeeze.
This approach changed my teaching. It allowed me to create lesson sequences where lower-attaining students could make the same progress as high-attainers
I found that debugging the code or tweaking the AI-generated slides took just as long, if not longer, than making the slides manually.
